transcript: Last spring I was the on-call engineer when our checkout started failing for about eight percent of payments, mostly on mobile. It was a Friday evening and every failed payment was lost revenue, so my goal was to find the cause within the hour. First I checked the error dashboard and saw the failures started at 18:05, which matched a deploy of the payment service. I didn't roll back straight away, because the same deploy contained a tax fix that finance needed that night. Instead I compared failing and successful requests in the logs and noticed that every failure had a card-holder name longer than 26 characters. A validation library we had just added trimmed the name, and the payment provider rejected the trimmed value because it no longer matched the card. I wrote a two-line fix that skipped trimming for that field, added a test with a 40-character name, and shipped it at 18:50. Failures dropped back to the normal rate of about 0.3 percent within ten minutes. On Monday I wrote the incident review and proposed contract tests against the provider's sandbox for every field we transform. We added them the next sprint, and two months later they caught a similar problem with postcodes before it reached users.
notes: Complete STAR, numbers, clear I, prevention and a later payoff.

transcript: So there was this time when our checkout was failing for some users. It was pretty urgent because, you know, it was payments. We looked at the logs and the dashboards to figure out what was going on, and it turned out it was related to a deploy we'd done earlier that day, something to do with how we validated the card holder name. We fixed the validation and deployed again and after that it was working. I think it took us maybe an hour or so. Afterwards we talked about it in the retro and decided we should have better tests for the payment flow, so we added some tests. I learned that it's important to check recent deploys first when something breaks, and also to stay calm under pressure, because panicking doesn't help anyone.
notes: Right story, but mostly 'we', vague cause and result, generic lesson.

transcript: I shipped a filter panel for a fictional stock dashboard. I assumed users would set several filters and then press Apply, because that reduced requests. In the first week, support received twelve reports saying filters were broken. I watched three users try it and saw that they changed a checkbox and immediately read the unchanged table; they never noticed Apply below the fold. I owned that interaction, so I reproduced it on a short laptop screen and checked the original usability notes. We had tested only a tall desktop layout. I changed the panel to apply changes automatically after a short debounce and kept the selected filters visible above the table. To avoid excessive requests, I cancelled stale requests and cached repeated combinations. I added a test that rapid changes only displayed the latest result. Then I asked the same three users to repeat their tasks, and all three finished without prompting. In the next two weeks the related support reports fell from twelve to one. I learned to test at the actual screen size and to watch what people expect before optimising the network path.
notes: Concrete explanation, personal decisions, trade-offs and validation appropriate to the stated level.

transcript: I worked on a dashboard where users could filter a table. We put an Apply button underneath the filters, but some people thought the checkboxes would update the results straight away. Support told us about it after launch. I helped move the controls around and we made the filters update automatically. We checked it ourselves and asked a couple of people whether it looked better. They seemed happier with it. I think the lesson was that we should ask users earlier, and I would probably do more testing next time. I don't remember whether we measured the number of support reports after the change.
notes: Relevant answer with an identifiable approach, but limited validation and vague results.

We listened to the feedback and made it more user friendly. I always try to be flexible about changes. The important thing is to keep improving it and make sure everyone is happy with the result. transcript: I treat an endpoint as idempotent when repeating the same operation has the same intended effect as doing it once. The HTTP response can differ, but a retry must not create a second payment. I would have the caller generate a stable idempotency key for one purchase attempt and reuse it across network retries. On the server I would scope that key to the account and store a hash of the relevant request fields. A unique constraint would make claiming the key atomic, so two concurrent requests cannot both start the payment. If a key is reused with a different amount, I would reject it rather than quietly returning an unrelated result. For the provider call I would forward the stable key if the provider supports it. I would record pending and completed states and return the saved result for a completed operation. A timeout after the provider charges is the awkward case: I would reconcile the provider status using that key instead of blindly charging again. I would test concurrent duplicate requests, changed payloads and a connection failure after a successful charge. For expiry, I would document the retry window and retain the deduplication record long enough to cover it.
notes: Concrete explanation, personal decisions, trade-offs and validation appropriate to the stated level.

transcript: I understand idempotency as getting the same effect when a client retries a request. For a payment I would send a unique request ID and store it with the payment record. When the same ID arrives again, I would return the existing payment instead of creating another one. I would also ask the provider to use that ID if they support it. I would test sending the request twice and check that there is only one charge. I haven't worked through exactly what happens if two requests arrive at the same time or if the provider succeeds but our database write fails. Those are things I would investigate before releasing it.
notes: Relevant answer with an identifiable approach, but limited validation and vague results.

transcript: I think idempotent means an endpoint is reliable and can handle requests consistently. For payments I would make sure the code checks everything carefully and returns an error if something goes wrong. I would probably retry a failed request a few times because networks are unreliable. I would also add logging so the team could find problems. I know duplicate payments would be bad, so I would try to check whether a payment already exists before making another one, but I haven't thought about how that check works.

transcript: I would start by defining what the feature promises and which mistakes are unacceptable. For a support-draft feature, I would separate factual correctness, source support, usefulness and tone rather than asking whether a reply just sounds good. I would collect fictional or permissioned examples covering common questions, missing information and malicious instructions in retrieved text. I would keep a held-out set so I don't tune only to the examples I can see. Two reviewers would score an initial sample with the same rubric, compare disagreements and tighten unclear criteria. I would then run the same set against a baseline and each prompt change, measuring schema validity, unsupported claims and refusal behaviour as well as rubric scores. I would set release thresholds before looking at the candidate results, with no tolerated fabricated policy instructions in the safety cases. I would track latency and cost too, because a good draft that arrives too late is not useful. I would first ship to a small opt-in group with human review, inspect corrections and add new failure cases to the evaluation set. An increase in unsupported claims would trigger rollback even if the average quality score improved.
notes: Concrete explanation, personal decisions, trade-offs and validation appropriate to the stated level.

transcript: I would make a list of example questions and expected answers, then run the model on them after changing the prompt. I would review whether the answers were relevant and whether the output format was correct. I would also measure response time and roughly how much each call cost. Before shipping I would ask a few teammates to try it and tell me which answers were wrong. I would compare the new version against the old one on the same questions. I haven't decided a numerical release threshold or how I would keep the test set separate from the examples used while editing the prompt. I would probably start with a small release and watch feedback.
notes: Relevant answer with an identifiable approach, but limited validation and vague results.

transcript: I usually try a model with a few questions and see if the answers read well. If they look accurate and helpful then I think it is probably ready for people to try. I would ask the team what they thought too, because everyone has a different opinion about good writing. I know models sometimes make mistakes, so I would put a warning near the feature and improve the prompt if someone complained. I don't have a particular way of measuring whether one version is better than another.
notes: Generic claims without an actionable explanation or evidence of personal decisions.

transcript: I would put a server endpoint between the browser and the model so the provider key never reaches the client. The browser submits a conversation ID and a new message ID. The server authenticates access, checks limits and starts the model request. I would use a streamed response with typed events for text chunks, completion and failure, each carrying a sequence number. The browser appends chunks to one message and marks it complete only after the completion event, not merely when the connection closes. I would cancel the provider request when the client disconnects unless the product explicitly needs background completion. For a dropped connection I would keep the partial text visible with an interrupted status and offer retry. If resumable streams are required, I would retain a bounded event buffer on the server and let the client reconnect with the last acknowledged sequence, deduplicating repeated events. Without that buffer I would explain that retry starts a new generation; I wouldn't pretend the model can continue with identical text. I would bound connection duration and output size and test drops before the first chunk, midway through a chunk and after completion. I would measure time to first text separately from total generation time.
notes: Concrete explanation, personal decisions, trade-offs and validation appropriate to the stated level.

transcript: I would have the browser call our server and the server call the model. The server would stream text back as it arrives, probably using server-sent events. In the browser I would append each chunk to the answer and show a loading indicator until it finishes. I would keep the API key on the server and check the user can access the chat. If the connection drops I would show an error and a retry button. I would test it with a slow network. I haven't decided whether a retry resumes the old response or starts a fresh one, or how to avoid duplicated text after reconnecting.
notes: Relevant answer with an identifiable approach, but limited validation and vague results.

transcript: I would use a frontend chat component and connect it to a backend that talks to the model. Streaming should make it feel fast because users see text appearing. I think a library could handle most of the difficult parts. If the connection drops I would reconnect and try again. I would add some error handling and make sure it worked on mobile. I haven't designed the message format or thought much about what happens to the half finished response, but I would investigate that while implementing it.
notes: Generic claims without an actionable explanation or evidence of personal decisions.

transcript: During a training project I was responsible for a small event signup page that had to work for a demonstration on Thursday. On Tuesday I realised the optional animated preview and custom calendar would take longer than I had estimated. I listed the remaining work with my mentor and asked which parts the demonstration actually needed. The essential flow was selecting an event, entering contact details and receiving confirmation. I proposed keeping a native date input and dropping the animation, while preserving validation and keyboard access. I wrote the reduced checklist in the project notes so the person giving the demonstration knew what to expect. I finished the form on Wednesday, then used the remaining time to test invalid email addresses, double submission and a narrow screen. The demonstration completed the signup flow without a failure. Afterwards I compared my estimate with the time spent and saw I had forgotten testing time. On my next task I included that explicitly and flagged uncertain work before promising a date. I didn't make the priority decision alone; my contribution was identifying the risk early and offering a concrete smaller scope.
notes: Concrete explanation, personal decisions, trade-offs and validation appropriate to the stated level.

transcript: I had to finish a signup page for a project demonstration and there wasn't enough time for all the features. I talked with my mentor and we agreed to leave out the animation and use simpler controls. I focused on the form and getting the confirmation page working. We tried it before the demonstration and it seemed fine. I think choosing the important features helped us finish on time. I don't remember exactly how we compared the priorities, and I didn't write down what we postponed. Next time I would try to estimate better and leave more time for testing.

transcript: I would use a composite index when a query repeatedly filters on two columns. I would look at the query plan and compare the rows scanned before and after adding it. The column order matters for the predicates and sorting the query actually uses. I would also measure write performance because each insert or update has to maintain the index. I wouldn't add indexes to every column just in case. I would start with a slow query from a representative workload and check that the improvement is worth the storage and maintenance cost.
notes: Technical indexing explanation does not answer the requested user-expectation story; off-topic caps apply.
